record.text: How do the projects that use chalcogenide phase-change materials such as GeSbTe to make metasurfaces switchable differ in their approaches?
record.reference_answer: The two differ in the optical platform the phase-change material is attached to and in how it is switched. SGPCM (705960) targets graphene plasmons, whose electric-gate tuning is volatile and slow, and controls the structural phase of the chalcogenide GeSbTe (GST) alloy to give them non-volatile, ultrafast, all-optical switching; it imaged CVD-grown graphene on thermally switched GST with a scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscope (s-SNOM) and found the plasmon wavelength on crystalline PCM shorter by a factor of two than on amorphous PCM, and it also produced a first hyperbolic mid-infrared metasurface from nanostructured hBN. DReM-PCM (896937) instead starts from all-dielectric metasurfaces, which it says are more efficient than plasmonic ones but fixed-by-design, and combines high-index dielectric nanoresonator arrays with GeSbTe alloys to tune the optical response continuously across crystalline, amorphous and intermediate states. Its distinguishing claim is the switching route: earlier phase-change metasurface designs were switched ex-situ, so DReM-PCM sets out to switch electrically in situ, by an integrated microheater and by a crossbar structure, for uses such as Lidar-type beam steering.

record.text: How do the approaches differ across projects that switch a chalcogenide phase-change material such as GeSbTe in order to change the optical response of a nanostructured photonic device?
record.reference_answer: All three switch a chalcogenide phase-change material to retune a nanoscale optical structure, but they differ in what carries the optical response and in how the material is switched. SGPCM (705960) puts the phase-change material under a two-dimensional conductor: it controls the structural phase of the chalcogenide GeSbTe (GST) alloy to give graphene plasmons the non-volatile, ultrafast, all-optical switching that volatile, slow electric-gate tuning cannot, imaging CVD-grown graphene on thermally switched GST with a scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscope (s-SNOM) and measuring a plasmon wavelength on crystalline PCM shorter by a factor of two than on amorphous PCM. DReM-PCM (896937) instead combines GeSbTe with high-index dielectric nanoresonator arrays to make an all-dielectric metasurface - more efficient than a plasmonic one but otherwise fixed-by-design - reconfigurable, and its distinguishing move is the switching route: where earlier phase-change metasurfaces were switched ex-situ, it switches electrically in situ with an integrated microheater and with a crossbar structure, tuning continuously for uses such as Lidar-type beam steering. PHEMTRONICS (899598) is the most device-oriented and the most optically driven of the three: a transdimensional, low-loss plasmonic platform of photo-switchable phase-change chalcogenides in which light itself triggers the phase transformation of active nanoantennas, targeting femtosecond-scale switching at femtojoule/bit for reconfigurable photonic systems, adaptive multiple-band photodetectors and an all-optical spiking neuron circuit.

record.text: How do the projects that use cosmic-ray muon imaging to inspect the contents of sealed containers and vehicles without opening them differ in what each is trying to detect inside?
record.reference_answer: Three projects apply cosmic-ray muon imaging to closed containers, and each is looking for something different. IMPRINT, built around Lingacom's Muon Detection System, reconstructs 3D imaging from muon data to find high-Z materials used in nuclear bombs and shielded radioactive materials (the 'dirty bomb' case) inside containerized cargo and vehicles leaving nuclear and radioactive sites, precisely where radiation portal monitors and X-ray fail on dense or shielded loads. SilentBorder develops a cosmic-ray tomography (CRT) scanner for border guards, customs and LEAs that gives a visualised 3D image and distinguishes materials, targeting hazardous and illegal goods (e.g. SNM), contraband such as tobacco or explosives, and hidden persons in up to 20' iso containers and trucks.

record.reference_answer: Two projects have the muon scanner itself as their central objective, and they aim it at different threats. record.reference_answer: Two projects have the muon scanner itself as their central objective, and they aim it at different threats. IMPRINT is built around the innovative Muon Detection System that Lingacom is developing, using high-energy natural atmospheric cosmic ray muon particles to look for high-Z materials used in nuclear bombs and shielded radioactive materials (used in 'dirty bombs') in containerized cargo and vehicles - the case where Radiation Monitors and X-ray fail on dense or high attenuating vehicles - and it reconstructs 3D imaging from muon data, with the aim of stopping insiders stealing material from nuclear and radioactive sites. SilentBorder develops and validates a cosmic-ray tomography (CRT) scanner for border guard, customs and LEAs whose target is much broader smuggling: hazardous and illegal goods (e.g. SNM), contraband such as tobacco or explosive, and hidden persons in up to 20' iso containers, exploiting the fact that cosmic-ray muons are highly penetrating, about 10,000 times the energy of a typical X-ray, to distinguish materials and give a visualised 3D image. So IMPRINT is a nuclear-security instrument narrowed to shielded high-Z material, while SilentBorder is a customs instrument that also has to find organic contraband and people.
